name: Vivace RF microneedling

lead: Vivace is an RF microneedling device offered in aesthetic clinics, used by people who want tighter, smoother skin and better texture.

Like others in the category, it pairs needle punctures with radiofrequency energy to prompt collagen remodeling. No study located names the Vivace device itself; a registered 2023 trial examined fractional microneedling RF as a category for facial aging.

paras: It is performed in a clinic by a trained provider in a short session, typically repeated in a series. Skin tightening and texture changes appear gradually as the skin heals and remodels.

Redness and swelling are expected for a few days after treatment. Infection is a general microneedling concern when procedures are done without proper infection control. Device-specific risks are not documented in the available sources.

angle.text: Vivace is used for tighter, smoother skin and better texture. Needle punctures plus radiofrequency energy prompt collagen remodeling as the skin heals. No study located names the Vivace device itself; a trial has looked at the wider category.

lead: Vivace is a radiofrequency (RF) microneedling device made by Aesthetics Biomedical of Phoenix, Arizona, and used in clinics for skin tightening, smoother texture and fewer fine lines. In a Vivace session, a handpiece pushes fine needles into the skin and delivers RF energy at depth, which the company says stimulates natural collagen production. [1][2]
The company's announcements say physicians using it report benefits for facial wrinkles, fine lines, skin texture, tightening and toning of the face and neck, and overall glow. [1]

Microneedling in general is a cosmetic procedure in which sterile needles repeatedly puncture the skin, used for scarring and acne. [3] No published study located for this entry names the Vivace device specifically; a registered trial compared fractional microneedling radiofrequency, as a category, with facial muscle exercises. [4]
infobox: FDA clearance for electrocoagulation and hemostasis, October 2022 [2]

paras: Aesthetics Biomedical announced FDA clearance for use of the Vivace RF Microneedling device at both 1 MHz and 2 MHz, with 1 MHz remaining the basis of its standard Vivace treatment protocol and 2 MHz offered as an optional setting. The announcement did not list formal indications and describes a precision robotic motor and an insulated microneedle. [1]

In October 2022 Practical Dermatology reported that the FDA cleared the Vivace Ultra, an upgrade of the legacy device that combines RF microneedling with ultrasound imaging, for dermatologic and general surgical procedures for electrocoagulation and hemostasis. A national rollout was planned for early 2023. [2] That clearance is for those surgical uses and is distinct from any cosmetic claim.

Microneedling by hand tools or devices punctures the skin with tiny needles; it is used for scarring and acne, and sometimes combined with platelet-rich plasma, whose efficacy Wikipedia describes as still unproven. [3] RF microneedling adds radiofrequency energy delivered through the needles; the manufacturer says this stimulates collagen. [1]

Wikipedia notes that the main concern with microneedling in non-medical settings is operators lacking infection-control training, especially with PRP; New Mexico health officials warned of blood-borne infection risks, and in April 2024 the CDC reported HIV diagnoses among patients of one spa offering vampire facials. [3] A consumer article reported that the FDA had issued a warning about RF microneedling associated with burns and scarring; that claim was not verified against FDA's own page.

No studies found specifically on the Vivace device. Related category-level research: a 40-participant registered trial begun in 2023 compared facial muscle exercises with fractional microneedling radiofrequency for facial rejuvenation in people with facial aging; it is listed as completed, and its outcome data were not located. [4]
